cards.headline: Iraq’s top court rules federal government can take over Kurdish borders and oil fields

pages.text: Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has ruled that the federal government can deploy troops to the country’s international borders, including within the semi-autonomous Kurdish region. The ruling also allows the federal oil ministry to oversee and audit oil and gas fields, while Baghdad shares responsibility for managing the production of those resources with regional governments and producing provinces, according to state television. Federal authorities may also oversee agencies operating at all border crossings, including those in northern Iraq’s Kurdish region, though they must coordinate with regional and provincial governments regarding customs administration. This decision follows an order from Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi for federal forces to take over Kurdish-run border crossings and a demand for authority over oil fields currently controlled by Kurdish security forces in an effort to curb oil smuggling. The Iraqi government has not specified how or when this takeover will be implemented.

Kurdish authorities have denounced the move, with the regional government calling the attempt to take over borders and oil fields an “assault” on the region’s “constitutional rights.” Renad Mansour, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme and director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, stated that Iraq’s judiciary is “very much supportive” of the government’s campaign to establish a centralized political order. While the court's decision is seen as a victory for Prime Minister al-Zaidi, analysts suggest implementing moves against the Kurds and heavily armed Shia militias loyal to Iran will be challenging. This development follows an incident one week prior in which al-Zaidi ordered troops to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold for the Iran-aligned Shia militia Kataib Hezbollah, following allegations of oil smuggling. After initially responding with defiance, Kataib Hezbollah allowed soldiers into the city following a compromise brokered by Shia politicians.

cards.headline: Drone strikes in Sudan's Blue Nile State kill at least 14 people

pages.text: Paramilitary drone strikes in the Blue Nile State of Sudan killed at least 14 people, including children, in the southeastern city of Al-Damazin, according to a medical source and an NGO. A source from the Sudanese army told AFP that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted residential neighborhoods in Al-Damazin with several drones on November 24, 2026. The UN condemned the strikes, stating they killed 17 civilians in the state capital, Ed Damazin. Different sources provided varying casualty counts for the attacks in the region: a medical source reported at least 14 dead and 15 wounded; the NGO Emergency Lawyers reported 19 civilians killed, including 6 women, and 20 others injured across the cities of Al-Damazin and Roseires; the Sudanese Human Rights Observatory reported at least 19 civilians killed and nearly 25 others wounded, alleging the RSF launched more than 30 explosive drones at residential neighborhoods and facilities. The RSF has not commented on the reported casualties, and the army has not commented on RSF claims regarding the strikes.

The attacks occurred amid escalating violence in Blue Nile State, located along the border with Ethiopia, as the RSF attempts to seize control of the state capital, Al-Damazin. On November 24, 2026, an assault also targeted the city of Roseires, striking a dam, power generation facilities, and electrical infrastructure, which Emergency Lawyers said threatens to cut off electricity supplies to the region. The UN reported that RSF advances through Blue Nile State over the past few months have sent more than 100,000 people from surrounding villages fleeing into Al-Damazin. UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric reminded all parties to the conflict that civilians and civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law and must not be targeted. He also demanded that all sides facilitate immediate, safe, and sustained humanitarian access to those in need.

The drone strikes are part of a war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary RSF that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since April 2023. In a separate diplomatic development, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' personal envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, participated in consultations organized by the Quintet. The Quintet is a group comprising the UN, the African Union, IGAD, the Arab League, and the EU. The meeting included the Sudan Founding Alliance, a coalition known as Tasis that includes the RSF, and was intended to address concerns and clarify questions raised by the alliance.

cards.headline: Iraqi Prime Minister orders nationwide troop deployment to close oil smuggling routes

pages.text: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi, who also serves as the armed forces commander-in-chief, has ordered the deployment of military forces across all provinces to secure designated areas and close informal routes used for oil smuggling, according to the Defense Ministry. Defense Ministry spokesman Maj. Yahya Rasool told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that military units are being deployed to secure various areas, including Kirkuk. Rasool added that designated military brigades have been instructed to close informal routes identified along oil smuggling corridors and noted that Iraqi army units stationed in Kirkuk are already carrying out the directives. The Defense Ministry stated it is fully prepared to implement all assigned missions as part of an intensified government crackdown on smuggling and efforts to strengthen state control over security operations.

The orders follow a government intelligence report published by the INA on November 24, 2026, which identified oil smuggling routes running from the Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah provinces to Iran and onward to Afghanistan. The report described operations intended to conceal the Iranian origin of petroleum products by falsely labeling them as Iraqi.

cards.headline: Huawei found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud in US trial

pages.text: A jury in a Brooklyn court has found the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, and conspiracy to violate US sanctions. While the company was convicted of these charges, jurors declined to convict Huawei of a racketeering conspiracy charge, which would have required finding that the firm acted as a criminal enterprise. Following the verdict, Huawei stated that the racketeering acquittal “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis” and said it would “take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”

The two-month trial involved allegations from federal prosecutors that Huawei spent 20 years using deceptive practices to gain a competitive advantage. Assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors that the company lied to banks regarding its business dealings in Iran and stole technology secrets from rival firms. US Attorney General Todd Blanche stated that Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted business in the United States on the basis of “lies and theft.” In response, Huawei's defence team argued that the firm's success was due to its own innovation and suggested that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built their case around that premise.

The legal proceedings follow a series of events beginning in late 2018 with the arrest of senior executive Meng Wanzhou, also known as Cathy Meng, in Canada. Meng was held in Canada for three years before being released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors. Federal prosecutors first announced the formal charges against Huawei in 2019.

cards.headline: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway

pages.text: At least 31 people were killed and at least 21 others were injured after a fuel tanker overturned and ignited a massive fire on the Ring Road in Giza, Egypt, on November 25, 2026. The Ring Road is a major highway that encircles the Greater Cairo metropolitan area. The crash occurred in the Waraq district, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza, leaving more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred in the blaze. Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar stated that the death toll is preliminary and expressed concerns that it could rise further. He noted that 39 ambulances responded to the accident and that the injured were transported to nearby hospitals.

The public prosecutor’s office has launched an investigation into the crash and confirmed that DNA investigations are underway to identify victims who were badly burned. During the rescue efforts, workers were seen pulling people from burning vehicles as firefighters worked to contain the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Waraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. Egyptian President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi issued a statement expressing his condolences to the victims and directing authorities to provide support to the families of the deceased and the injured. International officials, including Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, and Algerian Ambassador to Egypt Mohamed Sofiane Berrah, also expressed solidarity and condolences.

The accident occurred on a highway known for frequent traffic incidents, which claim thousands of lives annually in Egypt. Authorities attribute many of these crashes to speeding, poor road conditions, and the lax enforcement of traffic laws and safety rules.

cards.headline: US Education Department launches investigation into Virginia schools following sexual abuse scandal

pages.text: The United States Department of Education is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a school district in Albemarle County, Virginia, following a child sexual abuse scandal involving employees. The move comes after local officials closed all 29 schools in the district after discovering that more than 500 staff members had not undergone routine background screenings for a history of child sexual abuse. Local officials stated that none of the 524 employees identified in the screening failure is suspected of abuse. The school system employs approximately 2,800 people and operates with a $284m budget, though only a fraction of that budget is provided by the federal government. US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on November 24, 2026, that parents should not have to question if a school is aiding child predators, adding that the Trump administration is taking enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable.

The scandal in Albemarle County has led to several criminal and administrative consequences. According to the Albemarle County Police Department, a former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material, and a counsellor at another school was indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children after being placed on leave. Additionally, a school principal and two county school officials were charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned. The shutdown of the schools, which serve approximately 14,000 students, forced parents to seek alternative childcare and left many students who rely on free school meals without their usual food sources. Albemarle school board member Bob Beard told Al Jazeera that while families struggled with the shutdown, the schools were scheduled to reopen on November 23, 2026.

cards.headline: World experiences first six-day streak of temperatures 2C above preindustrial levels

pages.text: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, according to information obtained by the Guardian. On November 23, 2026, the daily global surface temperature reached 2.24C above the 1850-1900 baseline, the highest ever recorded for a single day. This temperature spike is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. This record-breaking streak follows two previous periods where daily temperatures climbed over 2C, occurring in November 2023 and February 2024, though neither lasted as long or reached such high levels as the current spell. Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, stated that the previous record of 2.05C above the baseline set in 2023 has been “smashed.”

The current temperature anomaly is being driven by an unusually large El Niño, a climate pattern approaching its peak, alongside long-term global heating caused by human fossil fuel combustion. Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the Copernicus Climate Change Service, described the event as an “exceptional global temperature anomaly,” noting that while individual days fluctuate, temperatures at this level indicate how much the climate has heated. Scientists expect the current El Niño to peak between now and January, though its full impact may not be felt for several months. Burgess noted that the last El Niño on this scale occurred in the 1870s and was associated with a mass famine that killed 50 million people. The extra heat in the global system is already contributing to climate feedbacks, including drought and fire in the Amazon and the tropical rainforests of Indonesia.

While this record hot streak is too brief to confirm that the upper limit of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, scientists warned it serves as an early indication of future conditions unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. The development also feeds into scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. Burgess stated that record global temperatures have persisted for several months, and the current streak represents a striking indication of the scale of climate heating.

cards.headline: Alberta legislature passes legislation for new electoral riding maps amid NDP legal threat

pages.text: The Alberta legislature has passed debate on legislation to implement new electoral riding maps, a move the Opposition NDP says will trigger a court battle. The new maps will create hybrid ridings by merging some urban areas in Calgary and Lethbridge with surrounding rural areas. NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has alleged the changes favor the governing United Conservative Party by diluting the power of urban votes, and he stated the NDP would launch a legal challenge regarding the proposal.

The proposed maps include several specific changes to district compositions and populations. In Lethbridge, two existing urban ridings are set to become four, consisting of one strictly urban district and three sprawling hybrid ridings that, in some instances, stretch to the U.S. border. Additionally, urban ridings in Calgary and Edmonton are set to be approximately six per cent more populated on average than other ridings in the province, while rural ridings are to be consistently underpopulated.

Premier Danielle Smith's government has denied allegations that it is seeking an unfair advantage for the 2027 election. The government stated that the task of redrawing the maps was left to a special panel and argued that the new maps will boost effective representation. Government officials also noted that hybrid ridings already exist in other parts of the province. The controversy escalated during the fall sitting when Speaker Ric McIver removed deputy NDP leader Rakhi Pancholi from the house for the day after she used the term 'cheating' to describe government actions. McIver ruled the term was out of order, while Pancholi stated she was standing up for Albertans.

cards.headline: Houthis target Saudi Arabian Red Sea ports as strikes escalate

pages.text: Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, marking a further escalation in conflict between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi Arabia. On November 25, 2026, a Saudi-led military coalition reported that a Houthi attack on Jizan caused minor damage and no civilian casualties, adding that efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile used. The Houthis claimed that strikes on both Jizan and the port of Jeddah resulted in damage. Earlier on November 25, 2026, the Houthis had threatened to attack Saudi ports if the port of Hodeidah in Yemen came under attack. Hodeidah, which is controlled by the Houthis, handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen; Al Jazeera reporter Yousef Mawry noted that if the port is closed, the humanitarian situation could be brought to the brink of collapse. Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV had reported new Saudi attacks on Hodeidah prior to the port strikes.

The escalation includes multiple strikes targeting Saudi Arabian infrastructure. On November 25, 2026, the Saudi-led coalition stated its air defenses intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the capital, Riyadh. Following this announcement, an explosion was heard in Sanaa, Yemen, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi. Additionally, Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the coalition, stated on X that Saudi forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over the port of Jeddah, noting that no civilian injuries were reported from falling debris. These incidents follow a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on November 24, 2026, which injured at least 11 people. The Houthis also claimed responsibility for attacks on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery; Argus Media reported that the Houthis landed two successful blows on the facility, one at the refinery and one at the export terminal.

The conflict involves ongoing military and diplomatic maneuvering. While Arab and Western officials told Middle East Eye that Saudi Arabia is shooting down the majority of Houthi missiles and drones, the kingdom has failed to protect certain assets such as airports, financial centers, and energy facilities. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought regional and international support; Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey, and Syria have committed or sent military support, though Syria's assistance is limited to drone operators. The US, Saudi Arabia's top military supplier, has not publicly committed additional support, though it maintains troops and advisers in the country. Amid the strikes, Semafor reported on November 25, 2026, that Mohammed bin Salman will travel to the US for the G-20 summit in Miami. Separately, on November 25, 2026, Iran reported via the Fars news agency that an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted zone in the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: South African court convicts Zimbabwean man for attempting to join Russian military

pages.text: A South African court convicted and sentenced Tafadzwa Sithole, a Zimbabwean man, for attempting to travel to Russia to fight in its war against Ukraine. Sithole, an unemployed third-year university student in Zimbabwe, was sentenced on November 24, 2026, to five years of imprisonment, which has been suspended for five years. He is set to be deported to Zimbabwe. He was arrested on November 8 at O.R. Tambo International Airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia alongside eight others. Sithole entered South Africa legally on November 4 and stayed in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, to prepare for his travel.

Sithole pleaded guilty to violating South Africa’s Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, a law that prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training. In a plea agreement with South African prosecutors, Sithole stated he completed an online application in Zimbabwe to fight for Russia in exchange for “remuneration.” Following the application, he said he was contacted by an individual he identified as “Albina,” who arranged his accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia. Sithole appeared in court on December 1, 2026, with four other accused individuals who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.

cards.headline: Unions call off sit-in amid labor dispute at Indonesia's largest nickel hub

pages.text: Unions representing approximately 10,000 workers have called off a five-day sit-in at government labor department offices in the Morowali district of Central Sulawesi province, Indonesia. The sit-in, involving the Federation of Independent Industrial Workers’ Unions (FSPIM), the Indonesian Morowali Industrial Labor Union (SBIMI), and the Mining and Energy Industry Labor Unions (SBIPE), was intended to prevent employers from filing a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) with the government. A CBA is a negotiated contract between employers and workers that establishes terms of employment. Union leaders stated the sit-in aimed to forestall the agreement from being brought into force. Workers have been without a new collective agreement since 2023, after talks to replace the previous contract collapsed. The Morowali labor department extended the existing contract until it expires in November 2025. The dispute centers on PT Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP), the world's largest conglomeration of nickel smelters. Majority-owned by China’s Tsingshan Holding Group, IMIP houses more than 50 companies and more than 100,000 workers, processing nickel into stainless steel and materials for electric vehicle batteries and renewable energy storage.

cards.headline: Bangladesh seeks water-flow guarantee as Ganges treaty nears expiry

pages.text: Bangladesh is calling for a guaranteed water-flow provision in a new Ganges water-sharing agreement with India as the current 30-year treaty is set to expire on December 12. With less than three weeks remaining before the expiration, no formal negotiations for a renewal or replacement have yet begun. Bangladesh authorities stated they are ready for talks and want a stronger agreement to protect its fair share of water, particularly during the dry season when river flows decline. Water Resources Minister Md Shahid Uddin Chowdhury Anee told BSS that the country wants to secure its legitimate share through a new arrangement. He noted that restoring a guarantee clause, similar to the one used in a 1977 agreement, is a priority. That 1977 clause ensured Bangladesh received at least 80 percent of its stipulated share during any 10-day period when water availability at Farakka during the dry season fell significantly. The current 1996 treaty did not include such a guarantee clause.

The existing treaty, signed on December 12, 1996, requires monitoring water flows at the Farakka Barrage in India and the Hardinge Bridge point in Bangladesh from January 1 to May 31 each year. Under the current sharing formula, water is allocated every 10 days based on the flow recorded at the Farakka point: if the flow is 70,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs) or less, the two countries share it equally; if the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh receives 35,000 cusecs and India takes the remainder; if the flow reaches 75,000 cusecs or more, India receives 40,000 cusecs and Bangladesh receives the rest. On November 22, 2026, the 91st regular meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint Rivers Commission (JRC) held in Dhaka finalized an annual report on the implementation of the Ganges water-sharing treaty for 2026, but treaty renewal was not discussed because such negotiations fall under the jurisdiction of the two governments and their political leadership. Dr Md Anwar Kadir, a member of the JRC and head of the Bangladeshi delegation, stated that regular information exchange, river-flow monitoring, and joint reviews are essential for effective implementation of the existing agreement.

Bangladesh has formed a high-level technical committee to prepare for negotiations, led by Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Professor Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir and including river experts and ministry representatives. Bangladesh formally proposed negotiations to India in June, and India requested the formation of a technical committee in August. On November 17, Water Resources Minister Md Shahid Uddin Chowdhury Anee sent another letter to his Indian counterpart urging an early start to negotiations. Under Article 12 of the Ganges treaty, the agreement remains effective for 30 years and can only be renewed by mutual consent. A proposed Teesta water-sharing agreement has yet to be signed despite years of discussions.

cards.headline: Israeli judges recommend dropping most serious bribery charges against Benjamin Netanyahu

pages.text: A judging panel at the Jerusalem District Court has suggested that prosecutors drop bribery charges against caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, citing a low probability of conviction in his most serious case. On November 25, 2026, the panel took the unusual step of summoning Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to express these concerns. Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told the Attorney General that the chances of conviction in the primary case are low enough to warrant reconsidering the matter, according to Israeli media reports. This development comes as Netanyahu faces three separate corruption cases involving allegations of granting government favors in exchange for positive media coverage. Netanyahu has consistently denied all allegations and, in a televised statement on November 25, 2026, called for the trial to end immediately, describing the proceedings as ten years of suffering for himself and his family.

The judicial recommendations specifically target Case 4,000, which involves an alleged reciprocal arrangement between Netanyahu and the controlling shareholder of Israel's largest telecommunications company. Both parties have denied any wrongdoing in that matter. Additionally, the judges questioned whether Netanyahu's actions in a second case, known as Case 2,000, met the threshold for criminal conduct. Case 2,000 involves an alleged quid-pro-quo with a different media baron. Regarding a third case, the judges suggested that prosecutors seek a plea deal. Netanyahu was first charged in 2019, though court proceedings have been prolonged in part by the recent Israel-Gaza war.

cards.headline: South Korea issues shelter warning to island residents as Russian warplanes approach airspace

pages.text: South Korea scrambled fighter jets and instructed residents of the eastern island of Ulleungdo to take shelter after Russian air force aircraft approached the country's territorial airspace. The interior ministry issued a warning at approximately 7:52 am local time, telling residents to move inside buildings or underground. The warning was lifted within minutes. According to the South Korean military, the aircraft entered the Korea Air Defence Identification Zone (ADIZ) and spent about 20 minutes inside the zone before turning away. An ADIZ is an area that extends beyond a country's national airspace and is used to identify approaching aircraft; entering the zone does not necessarily mean an aircraft has crossed into a country's territorial airspace. The Joint Chiefs of Staff stated that no violation of South Korean territorial airspace occurred. Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said the military issued the warning preemptively to protect the safety of the people because an airspace intrusion was anticipated.

The incident involved conflicting messages that caused confusion. An initial alert stated that Russian aircraft had entered South Korean airspace, while a subsequent message from North Gyeongsang provincial authorities misidentified the aircraft as possibly being North Korean. The military later clarified that the aircraft were Russian and had remained outside territorial airspace. This was the first time the South Korean military had issued a precautionary civilian alert regarding a possible airspace violation by Russian warplanes, according to the news agency Yonhap. In response, South Korea's defence ministry summoned Russia's military attaché, Colonel Nikolai Marchenko, to protest the incident and demand measures to prevent a recurrence. The ministry stated that repeated unannounced entries into the identification zone and the recent close approach could unnecessarily raise tensions across the region and on the Korean Peninsula. The foreign ministry also conveyed objections to Moscow through diplomatic channels.

Recent Russian aerial activity has also been reported in Poland and Japan. In Poland, officials reported a brief Russian drone incursion late on November 23, 2026, which turned east; authorities decided against shooting it down due to potential risks to civilians. This followed an incident on November 20, 2026, in which Polish prosecutors reported that three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland. In response to that missile incident, a NATO spokesperson confirmed on November 23, 2026, that the alliance authorized the deployment of an airborne early-warning aircraft to Poland, which uses radar to detect and track activity over a wide area. Separately, on November 19, 2026, Japan scrambled fighter jets after two aircraft believed to be Russian briefly entered its territorial airspace near Okinoshima, off Fukuoka, leading Tokyo to lodge a diplomatic protest with Moscow.

cards.headline: Two cancer patients sue Ontario over refusal to fund out-of-country treatments

pages.text: Two cancer patients have begun court proceedings against the Ontario government following the province's denial of funding for out-of-country medical treatments they describe as life-saving. Sabrina Apitz-Grossman, 31, and Kevin Nash, 59, are seeking T-cell therapy, a treatment that enables immune cells to better attack cancer. While the therapy is approved in the United States, it is not yet approved in Canada. Both Apitz-Grossman and Nash applied for out-of-country coverage through the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP), but the province denied their initial applications and subsequent appeals.

cards.headline: Bangladesh approves 36 per cent minimum wage hike for garment workers amid protests

pages.text: A government-appointed wage board in Bangladesh approved a 36 per cent increase to the minimum monthly wage for entry-level garment workers, raising it from 12,500 taka to 17,000 taka (approximately $136 USD or $193 CAD). The decision followed weeks of protests that included factory closures, highway blockades, property vandalism, and disrupted production in a sector that employs more than four million people and generates more than 80 per cent of the country's export earnings. The garment industry is a primary source of foreign currency for Bangladesh, with exports mostly directed to Europe and the United States to supply retailers such as H&M, Zara, Walmart, Target, and Gap.

The six-member wage board reached its decision around 2 a.m. local time after nearly 12 hours of discussions between representatives for workers and employers. The board approved the 17,000 taka minimum wage in a 4-2 vote; two members supported a worker demand of 18,000 taka ($204 CAD) per month, according to workers' representative Babul Akhter. This 36 per cent increase is the smallest percentage hike for the sector since the first minimum wage was established in 1986. For comparison, wages were raised by 77 per cent in 2013, 51 per cent in 2018, and 56 per cent in 2023. Anne Bienias, the living-wage co-ordinator for the Clean Clothes Campaign, stated that the new rate remains well below a living-wage level and that such negotiations result in poverty wages.

Tensions remained high following the announcement, as workers in Gazipur, a garment manufacturing hub on the outskirts of Dhaka, blocked a major highway. Police reported firing tear gas and sound grenades to disperse the demonstrators. The protests had previously led to clashes between police and workers, with police using batons to charge demonstrators. It was not immediately clear if workers would accept the new wage structure.

cards.headline: UN human rights chief warns of widening risk of atrocity crimes against Palestinians

pages.text: UN human rights chief Volker Türk has warned of a widening risk of further atrocity crimes by Israel against Palestinians, stating that recent violence in the occupied West Bank has heightened existential fears. Mr. Türk said his office has repeatedly warned that Israeli actions in Gaza pose a real threat to the continued existence of Palestinians as a group, and that recent events in the West Bank exacerbate the risk across the entirety of the occupied Palestinian territory. The High Commissioner stated that previous warnings have not been heeded and that atrocity crimes continue to recur.

According to the UN human rights office, since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks, 42,666 Palestinians have been forcibly displaced by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. In Gaza, nearly two million people have been forcibly displaced, often multiple times. Mr. Türk noted that civilians continue to be killed and that senior Israeli officials have indicated an intent for such displacement to be permanent. He expressed concern that Gaza’s population is being confined to an ever-shrinking sliver of the territory while Israel’s continued blockade and closure deprive Palestinians of food, medicine, and shelter.

Mr. Türk described the violations being perpetrated across both the West Bank and Gaza as increasingly widespread and systematic. He noted that civilian infrastructure is being destroyed in Gaza while illegal settlements advance in the West Bank. Additionally, he stated that Palestinians are persistently subjected to arbitrary detention, torture, mistreatment, and a two-tier justice system. Mr. Türk also expressed particular concern regarding continued unlawful killings in Gaza occurring after a ceasefire was announced.

cards.headline: US Attorney General declines to comment on potential Nvidia investigation

pages.text: US Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to confirm whether the AI chipmaker Nvidia is under federal investigation during a press engagement on November 24, 2026. While refusing to comment on specific inquiries into the company, Blanche described Nvidia as a “good corporate citizen.” He also stated he had no information regarding the security clearance status of Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang. Lawmakers are currently seeking answers regarding US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's return to the company. Huang was reinstated as CEO less than two weeks after being forced to resign following revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which involved an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress to face questioning regarding national security concerns. The inquiry focuses on his relationship with an alleged spy who previously managed Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia. The US commerce department has announced preparations to blacklist Megaspeed, which is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The commerce and justice departments stated they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. Regarding the status of these inquiries, Blanche told reporters on November 24, 2026, that the department has “hundreds, if not more” export investigations occurring at any one time.

President Trump has addressed the situation regarding Huang, telling the New York Post in an interview published on November 24, 2026, that he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he stated, “I don't think it'll be necessary.” When asked if he was satisfied that Nvidia had cooperated with inquiries into whether the company or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said he had no reason to suggest Nvidia was anything other than a good corporate citizen. Blanche noted that if Nvidia were the target of a criminal investigation or were obstructing an investigation, it would contradict the message being delivered by the president to the American people.

cards.headline: U.S. seeks to accommodate Canada on sectoral tariffs, official says

pages.text: A senior U.S. official told Reuters that the Trump administration intends to accommodate Canada regarding sectoral tariffs. This follows the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) announcing plans to impose new trade tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, and India. The administration accuses these economies of flooding world markets with cheap goods through subsidies and industrial policies that create what Washington calls “structural excess capacity.” According to a senior U.S. official, the USTR defines this capacity as countries promoting production and capacity that is divorced from market principles and the realities of demand.

The proposed duties follow an eight-month investigation by the USTR. China is expected to face the highest rates among the 14 targeted economies. The administration is utilizing Section 301 of a 1974 U.S. trade law to implement these tariffs, a mechanism that allows Washington to penalize countries it determines are treating U.S. businesses unfairly. Trump previously used Section 301 to place large tariffs on Chinese goods during his first term, which survived legal challenges in court. These new measures represent an attempt to rebuild sweeping import taxes after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down previous efforts in February.

The current tariffs are a response to the Supreme Court's ruling that an emergency powers law could not be used to impose trade tariffs. In April 2025, shortly after beginning his second term, Trump announced “Liberation Day” tariffs under that emergency law. Trade policy expert Dmitry Grozoubinski noted that the emergency law is intended for international economic emergencies, stating, “Tariffs are like taxes. You can’t really fight emergencies with mild taxes.”

cards.headline: Canadian auto sector shifting away from U.S. imports amid trade war

pages.text: The Canadian auto sector is pivoting away from United States imports toward other global markets due to an ongoing trade war, according to a report from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants. Data analysis shows that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total imports thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars. This is a decrease from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. During that same period, the market shares for Mexico, Japan, South Korea, and combined European markets all rose from two years ago.

DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King stated that certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible to continue providing Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price. The shift occurs amid significant tariff pressures. In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts, and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. Currently, vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content. Auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) are exempt from these tariffs. Canada maintains its own import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with CUSMA.

cards.headline: British Prime Minister authorizes inquiry into Cold War nuclear weapons tests

pages.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has authorized an independent inquiry into the impact of nuclear weapons tests on military veterans. The decision follows a 40-year campaign by survivors who claim they were used as test subjects during Cold War-era explosions, resulting in health damage to themselves and their children. Speaking on the BBC’s Newsnight program, Burnham stated that the panel’s chairman would be “relentless in his pursuit of the facts” and noted that the inquiry aims to establish the truth for veterans and their families. Between 1952 and 1967, an estimated 22,000 British military personnel witnessed nuclear weapons tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

Veterans allege that Britain’s Ministry of Defense intentionally concealed data from blood and urine samples. They claim this data would prove they were used as unwitting test subjects to study how nuclear explosions affect humans. Former Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood stated in the Guardian that the situation is “among the greatest scandals in Britain.” Ellwood noted that in 2018, he “inadvertently misled” Parliament by telling lawmakers the Ministry of Defense could not locate information regarding blood testing. He later learned that blood samples had been taken throughout the military, though veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses related to radiation exposure were unable to access them.

Unlike the United States, Britain has no dedicated compensation program for nuclear veterans. France has established a compensation program for tests conducted in Algeria and the South Pacific. The UK's involvement in nuclear testing began with its first atmospheric atomic test on Oct. 3, 1952, involving a plutonium implosion device in the Montebello Islands off Western Australia. That detonation made Britain the world’s third nuclear-armed nation, following the United States and the then-Soviet Union.

cards.headline: Ukraine says five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike

pages.text: Ukraine's General Staff said it damaged five Russian military aircraft during an attack on the Savasleyka airfield in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region. The strike hit three MiG-31s and two Su-34s at the facility, which is located approximately 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow. Kyiv stated that the extent of the damage is still being assessed but suggested there may be more news to come. The military did not specify what weapons were used in the attack. The Savasleyka airfield has been a target for Ukraine for several years and hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch glide bombs and hypersonic missiles. The takeoff of MiG-31s frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine because they carry Kinzhal missiles, which are difficult to shoot down and have been known to hit military targets and large infrastructure.

In a series of long-range strikes, Kyiv also reported hitting two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region, located approximately 800km (500 miles) from the front line. The Ukrainian defence ministry stated that these strikes are part of an effort to dent Moscow's oil processing capacity, adding, “Did you repair them? We'll hit them again.” Additionally, Kyiv reported hitting a radar system and fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia. The defence ministry said that successful hits on these targets aim to prevent the movement of military vehicles and the use of artillery by reducing available fuel and ammunition.

In the Samara region, governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev described overnight attacks as “a true ordeal,” reporting that more than 145 drones were shot down. Fedorishchev stated that one person was killed and several towns experienced power outages. Meanwhile, across Ukraine, local authorities reported that Russian attacks killed nine people and injured 59 others, including a 12-year-old child, over the past day. On November 24, 2026, the Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched 112 drones, including 66 jet-powered ones and decoys, overnight. As of 8 a.m. local time, air defenses had downed or suppressed 88 drones, including 47 jet-powered ones.

cards.headline: British household energy bills set to increase 26 percent in January

pages.text: British household energy bills are set to surge by more than a quarter in January, according to the sector regulator Ofgem. The increase follows a rise in wholesale gas prices driven by conflict in the Middle East. Ofgem, which sets a quarterly price cap on the amount electricity and gas suppliers can charge customers, announced the 26 percent increase to the cap will add approximately £443 ($580) to the typical annual bill, bringing it to about £2,166. This change will impact around 20 million households on standard contracts with variable tariffs, while a further 10 million households on fixed-rate deals will be shielded from the rise as long as their contracts remain in place.

The price surge is linked to the US-Iran conflict, which has sharply reduced tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Since the outbreak of the US-Iran war on 28 February, the price of European natural gas, measured by the Dutch TTF futures contract, has surged by around 190 percent, rising to 92 euros ($101) per megawatt-hour from around 32 euros. Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, stated that conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher and noted the increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches. The conflict has also contributed to Britain's annual inflation rate reaching a 12-month high of 3.6 percent in October as it drove up motor fuel costs.

The price hike means millions of households will face higher payments even after receiving direct subsidies of £100 toward energy bills. In its October annual budget report, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government announced the one-off payment for 20 million households and the removal of fixed fees on gas bills. The government has also extended a temporary tax cut on household electricity prices.

cards.headline: Indian nationals continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine

pages.text: Indian nationals are being drawn into the war in Ukraine through deception or desperation. While some seek employment, others join the Russian military under different circumstances, such as attempting to secure release from prison sentences in Russia. The Indian government faces questions regarding what it can do to protect its citizens from being sent to fight in the conflict.

One Indian national, Randhawa, told Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin that after arriving in Russia to find work as a driver, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract, and sent for training. Randhawa stated that his passport and phone were confiscated. He said he escaped from his unit and surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November, where he is currently being held as a prisoner of war. His account has not been independently verified. He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military.

In October 2025, Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces. Majothi had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.

cards.headline: Israeli airstrike kills senior Hamas security official and three family members in Gaza City

pages.text: An Israeli airstrike in the Gaza Strip killed Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry. The strike occurred at dawn in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City on November 24, 2026, causing extensive damage to the family's apartment. Photos of the site showed destroyed exterior and interior walls, with rubble and broken furniture scattered across the floor. The interior ministry stated that Abu al-Ouf, 47, was killed along with his wife, Noura, 41, and their two teenage daughters, Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13. The Israeli military described Abu al-Ouf as a “terrorist” and a “significant figure” who served as a “key source of expertise” in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza, stating he was eliminated “to remove the threat he posed.”

Hamas's internal security service is responsible for protecting the group's infrastructure, enforcing discipline, and rooting out informants. The interior ministry condemned the strike on the Abu al-Ouf family as a “heinous crime,” accusing Israel of targeting security personnel to “spread chaos within Palestinian society.” On November 24, 2026, Abu al-Ouf was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes. Other reported fatalities from strikes that day included three people, including a 17-year-old, in a separate strike near Gaza City, and three more people in a strike on a police station in the Al-Mawasi area of southern Gaza. Gaza's police force, which operates under Hamas, reported that two policemen, aged 23 and 33, were among those killed in the Al-Mawasi strike. The Israeli military said it had “struck terrorists in the area” of the police station but did not confirm the strike that reportedly killed the 17-year-old.

The strikes occurred despite a ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025. Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the truce, which followed two years of war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. Since the truce began, more than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed, according to data from Gaza's health ministry, which the United Nations considers reliable. During the same period, the Israeli military reports that seven of its soldiers and one civilian contractor have been killed. These developments come as Israel continues talks to form a new government following October legislative elections. Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister and in charge of military operations while centrist Gadi Eisenkot seeks to build a coalition to end Netanyahu's tenure.

cards.headline: IMF approves $425 million economic programme for Guinea

pages.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) approved a $425 million economic and financial programme for Guinea on November 23, 2026, to support economic reforms and strengthen public finance management over the next three years, according to the Guinean government. The programme is supported by the IMF's Extended Credit Facility and the Extended Fund Facility. This agreement follows an August 12 announcement that the IMF and the Guinean government had reached an agreement on an aid package totaling $439 million intended to strengthen the country's fiscal and monetary position. The approved $425 million is $14 million less than the amount outlined in that August agreement.

Guinean Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah described the negotiations as ``tough'' but welcomed the conclusion of the deal, stating it serves as a positive signal for the economy. Bah noted that the country seeks the IMF's oversight not only for funding but to access technical expertise and tools to steer the economy toward stronger performance. He also acknowledged that implementing the programme will be a challenge, requiring the administration to bolster its management and administrative capacities in the coming years. The partnership aims to boost domestic revenue mobilization, enhance budgetary transparency, and strengthen public financial management. The agreement arrives as Guinea attempts to accelerate economic growth through the Simandou 2040 development programme and the exploitation of the Simandou iron ore deposit. While rich in mineral resources such as bauxite and iron ore, Guinea has struggled to convert its natural wealth into economic and social benefits for its population.

cards.headline: China investigates Shanghai party chief Chen Jining

pages.text: China's state-run Xinhua news agency announced on November 24, 2026, that the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection is investigating Chen Jining, the Communist party chief of Shanghai and a member of the country's elite politburo. The watchdog is investigating Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” a term commonly used as a euphemism for corruption. For high-ranking officials, a public announcement of an investigation by this commission generally signals an eventual political downfall. The Shanghai city government stated that its Standing Committee expressed “firm support” for the decision to investigate Chen, adding that the move signals a determination to continue the fight against corruption. Chen, an environmental scientist who previously served as China's environmental protection minister and mayor of Beijing, has been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The position of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally served as a stepping stone to China's top leadership, previously held by President Xi Jinping, current premier Li Qiang, and former President Jiang Zemin.

The investigation into Chen marks the fourth member of the elite politburo to be probed since 2025. Before the announcement regarding Chen, three other members of the 24-member body formed in 2022—He Weidong, Zhang Youxia, and Ma Xingrui—had already been purged. He Weidong and Zhang Youxia were senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, while Ma Xingrui was a provincial party secretary. Analysts noted the investigation took them by surprise; on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo, the hashtag “Chen Jining under investigation” amassed approximately 240m views by morning, with users describing themselves as “shocked” and “stunned.” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School specializing in contemporary Chinese law and politics, described the development as arguably the biggest political news to come out of China in a few years. The probe represents a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party's senior leadership ranks and depleted the military's top command.

cards.headline: Syria prepares to appoint new diplomatic candidates in January

pages.text: Syria has lined up candidates to fill key positions at its diplomatic missions abroad in January, according to a Syrian Foreign Ministry source told The National. Since Bashar Al Assad was ousted from the presidency by rebels in December 2024, diplomats appointed during his rule have continued working in a caretaker capacity at many of Syria's embassies. The new government, which includes former commanders of Hayat Tahrir Al Sham (HTS)—the militant group that led the rebel offensive—is now moving to fill these roles. Current top officials include President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani. Some HTS members and newly appointed diplomats linked to the group have already been sent to embassies abroad as attaches, secretaries, and charges d'affaires. A charge d'affaires is a diplomat who heads a mission in the absence of an ambassador. The authorities have also reinstated experienced diplomats who defected from the former regime and have connections abroad, though very few were ambassadors.

The appointment of new diplomatic staff had been delayed because recruits required training and because some countries had objected to candidates proposed by the Foreign Ministry. A source stated that the history of some candidates was “problematic,” though the source did not elaborate. This delay reflects a challenge for the new authorities to present a moderate image while catering to supporters and former cadres of HTS, a group once affiliated with Al Qaeda. For the time being, Syria is only appointing charges d'affaires rather than the more senior rank of ambassador because the country is in a phase of political transition. Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani wants to “test the diplomats” first; once they prove themselves and host countries become “familiar” with them, it will be easier to promote them to ambassador. Among the sensitive postings is the charge d'affaires in Jordan, a position given to Saleh Muslet, a senior figure in the former western-recognised political opposition to the Assad regime from which HTS was excluded.

cards.headline: Low prosecution rates for wildlife crime in Nigeria as ivory and pangolin trafficking persists

pages.text: Nigeria remains the primary exit point for elephant ivory and pangolin scales destined for Asian markets, according to a report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). Between 2021 and 2026, authorities seized more than 50 metric tons of this contraband. Despite increased regional law enforcement operations, illegal wildlife trafficking continues to thrive across West and Central Africa, the EIA report states. Organized criminal syndicates have responded to intensified enforcement in major hubs like Lagos by shifting logistics to smaller port cities and concealing contraband within legal shipments, such as moringa seeds, Mongabay contributor Gloria Dickie reports.

Data from 58 documented wildlife crime incidents in Nigeria between January 2021 and February 2026 reveals significant gaps in the legal process. Out of 72 suspects involved in these incidents, only 19 were charged with a crime. Across six incidents, 12 individuals were convicted, resulting in an arrest-to-conviction rate of approximately 16%. Legal experts noted that while low-level poachers and couriers regularly face legal penalties, high-level network kingpins and facilitators frequently evade prosecution.

Justin Gosling, who leads the EIA program on securing criminal justice, noted that while Nigeria has seen its first prosecutions at this level, progress is limited. Gosling stated that five years ago, the country had not had any prosecutions for wildlife trafficking at that level. He argued that law enforcement agencies must target high-level organizers rather than fringe operatives to permanently disrupt syndicates, warning that picking off only individuals at the edge of networks allows them to bounce back. Ruth Musgrave, CEO of the Elephant Protection Initiative Foundation—the secretariat for a pan-African alliance working to conserve elephants and end the ivory trade—underscored the necessity for multifaceted regional strategies to combat the illegal trade.

cards.headline: More than 86,000 households in Gaza are now headed by women

pages.text: More than 86,000 households in Gaza are now headed by women, according to UN Women. This represents nearly one in four households, an increase from one in nine before the war. For many of these women, providing for a family involves managing food, shelter, water collection, and children's schooling from tents in displacement camps. At the Flowers of Palestine camp in western Gaza City, women and children carry buckets and plastic containers from water tankers back to canvas dwellings.

Kholoud Farajallah, a mother of three who lost her husband early in the war, told a UN News correspondent that women are performing the duties of both themselves and men. Due to a lack of income, Farajallah had to abandon her master’s degree in mathematics and teaching methods. She began baking pastries and sending her son to sell them around displacement camps to support her family.

cards.headline: Bird species diversity improves predator warning signals in forest communities

pages.text: Forest birds receive more effective warnings about predators when they live in habitats with higher species diversity. A study conducted across ten nature reserves in eastern China found that increased biodiversity strengthens the flow of ecological information, such as defensive calls used to alert others to danger or to recruit help to repel a threat. This suggests that in areas with reduced species richness, local prey may exhibit weaker responses to danger because the community's ability to transmit information is diminished.

Researchers led by Kumar conducted several hundred experiments to investigate how diversity impacts the transmission of defensive bird calls. In the first round of experiments, the team used models of flying hawks and sitting owls to trigger responses from prey birds. These birds responded with either alarm calls, which signal others to flee, or mobbing calls, which recruit other birds to gather around and harass a predator. In the second round, the team used a manipulative playback experiment, playing recorded mobbing calls through speakers and varying the number of species included in the sounds from one to eight species. The team found that increased species diversity in these recorded calls was strongly correlated with faster response calls and larger mobbing groups.

cards.headline: Malawi faces severe medical supply shortages as essential medicine availability drops to 40%

pages.text: A shortage of essential medicines in Malawi has forced patients to pay for basic supplies out of pocket, despite public healthcare being intended as free at the point of use. Internal reporting from the state-run Central Medical Stores Trust (CMST) shows that nationwide availability of essential medicines has fallen to 40%, a significant decrease from 77% in early 2025. In major referral hospitals, availability has dropped to as low as 18%.

In the Salima district, a fishing and farming region on the western shore of Lake Malawi, the shortage has left medical staff operating without basic supplies. At Salima hospital, the main public referral centre for a rural population of more than 500,000 people, frontline staff report that intravenous fluids have been completely unavailable for more than a week. Supplies of bandages, catheter bags, painkillers, and sterile gloves have been depleted for up to three months.

The scarcity of foreign exchange has paralyzed healthcare provision, according to reports. At Salima hospital, Maureen Msukwa, a 25-year-old pregnant mother from Kasache village, reported being instructed to buy paracetamol from a private vendor because the hospital pharmacy could not provide it. Evelyn Jossam, a 30-year-old nurse-midwife at the facility who requested anonymity, said relatives are sometimes forced to run outside to buy supplies immediately before a woman can be safely assisted during childbirth.

cards.headline: Gold and antimony deposits in northern Chad's Tibesti mountains drive regional conflict and illicit trade

pages.text: Gold and antimony deposits in the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad are central to a web of warfare and illicit trade involving Libya, Sudan, and the United Arab Emirates. The Tibesti, a remote volcanic range in the central Sahara that reaches 3,000 metres, runs through northern Chad and across the border into southern Libya. The mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory extends into southern Libya, northern Niger, and northwestern Sudan. While the valleys near the town of Miski contain vast gold deposits, the mountains also contain antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is exported in great quantities and is putting the Tubu ecosystem at severe risk.

The presence of gold has driven armed conflict between the Tubu and the Chadian and Libyan states for decades. This trade is linked to a network of warfare that stretches from Chad into Libya and Sudan, reaching the United Arab Emirates, where arms and supplies are flown to proxy armies, militias, and paramilitaries. On 14 October, armed clashes broke out in Miski. Following the fighting, the Chadian army’s general staff accused Miski’s self-defence committee—a local armed group descended from the Tubu institution of village guardianship—of breaking a peace agreement with the army by attacking the National Brigade for the Control of Mining Activities. The Chadian army issued an ultimatum to the Tubu group to lay down their arms or be treated as rebels.

cards.headline: Scientists find evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions 20,000 feet deep in the Mariana Trench

pages.text: Scientists have discovered signs of explosive volcanic eruptions approximately 20,000 feet underwater in the Mariana Trench, marking the deepest known instance of such activity on Earth. Using a remotely operated underwater vehicle, researchers recovered pyroclastic rocks—fragments of rock ejected during an eruption—and what they described as “abundant” evidence of ultradeep explosive volcanism. The findings were detailed in a study published November 22 in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science. This discovery occurred in the western Pacific Ocean at Challenger Deep, which is the deepest known point on Earth, reaching 35,876 feet below the water's surface. William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University who was not involved with the research, told Science News that the discovery is “surprising and unprecedented.”

The exploration of the Mariana Trench often requires robotic technology because the environment is dangerous for humans; at Challenger Deep, the pressure is roughly 1,000 times the pressure experienced at sea level. In 2024, researchers used a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution submersible named Jason/Medea to explore parts of the trench. While most exploration is conducted via robots, some individuals have reached Challenger Deep by submarine, including Navy officer Don Walsh and Swiss oceanographer Jacques Piccard in January 1960.

cards.headline: Smooth-coated otters spotted along Kuala Lumpur’s Klang River

pages.text: Increasing sightings of smooth-coated otters along the Klang River in Kuala Lumpur have raised hopes that long-term clean-up efforts are improving water quality and restoring urban wildlife habitats. Conservationists and city officials hope the presence of these otters can encourage further initiatives to clean the river, reduce waste entering the waterway, and restore more natural riverbanks.

The growing otter population has led to conflict in some areas. Habitat loss resulting from development has driven some otters into residential areas, where they have raided fish ponds. This has prompted calls for residents to adapt to the animals' presence rather than harming them, as the otters are protected.

cards.headline: Rising prices and renewed fighting strain families in Hodeidah, Yemen

pages.text: Families in the Houthi-controlled Red Sea port city of Hodeidah, Yemen, are struggling to afford basic goods due to rising fuel costs, shrinking incomes, and renewed fighting. The Hodeidah port serves as the primary entry point for commercial and humanitarian imports into Yemen’s Houthi-controlled northwest, but the city is facing increased economic pressure as more than a decade of war continues. Fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia intensified in July after four years of relative calm, with the Houthis making significant advances in Yemen’s southern Red Sea coast region. While the Hodeidah port has come under attack by the Saudi-led coalition, it remains open.

The economic strain is affecting residents' ability to secure daily necessities like flour, rice, and bread. Ahmed Arjash, a motorcycle taxi driver in his late 30s who supports a family of six, reported to Al Jazeera that his daily earnings now barely cover the fuel or the rent for his motorcycle. He noted that while he previously could save for repairs or medicine, he now sometimes returns home empty-handed or with insufficient food. In the al-Salkhana neighbourhood, Umm Sami, a widow raising four children, reported to Al Jazeera that she has been forced to buy food in very small quantities, such as flour or oil that lasts only one day, because she cannot afford whole bags.

cards.headline: Meta scientists develop AI to decode typed sentences from noninvasive brain activity

pages.text: Scientists at Meta have developed an artificial intelligence system that translates brain activity recorded outside the skull into typed sentences. According to a study published in Nature Neuroscience, the model decoded memorized sentences typed by healthy volunteers using magnetic brain scans. The system achieved an average character error rate of 29 percent, while the top-performing participant reached an 18 percent error rate. This approach aims to provide a safer alternative to brain-computer interfaces that require surgical implants.

Brain-computer interfaces are systems that use computer software to turn electrical or magnetic signals generated by active brain cells into digital text or device commands. Currently, the fastest systems are invasive neuroprostheses. These require neurosurgeons to open the skull and place electrode arrays directly onto or into the motor cortex, the area of the brain that plans and controls voluntary movement. While surgical implants have restored rapid text generation for people paralyzed by stroke, spinal cord injury, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the surgery carries risks of infection and bleeding. Additionally, keeping electrodes working reliably inside living tissue over long periods remains difficult.

Noninvasive interfaces attempt to avoid surgery by reading signals from outside the head. One common method is electroencephalography (EEG), which uses sensors on the scalp to measure electrical currents from brain cells. While the Meta AI system is less accurate than surgical chips, it represents a move toward communication tools that do not require brain surgery. For comparison, a 2021 clinical study of a man with hand paralysis used an implant to decode attempted handwriting at 90 characters per minute with a character error rate below 6 percent. Another implant trial involving a paralyzed patient translated attempted speech into text at 62 words per minute with 94 percent word accuracy.

cards.headline: UK forcibly resettled sex offender refugee to Eswatini in undisclosed deal

pages.text: The UK government forcibly resettled a Sri Lankan refugee and convicted sex offender to Eswatini, an African country with which he had no connection, through a deal that was not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community. The man, 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini. Peramalya had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts. He was originally rescued in 2021 by the Royal Navy in the Indian Ocean alongside dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers attempting to sail from India to Canada. Migration experts told the BBC this is the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling a refugee permanently overseas in this manner.

The BBC obtained a copy of a draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments, which states the UK pledges to cover the costs of Peramalya's resettlement for up to three years. At the time of his death, the UK government was finalising plans for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently. The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public is its priority and that it continues to work with Eswatini authorities regarding the case. While the Labour government scrapped a plan in 2024 to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda, it intends to send failed asylum seekers to third countries when they cannot be returned to their home countries, though it has not yet announced any such deals.

The Eswatini deal has drawn criticism from multiple sides. Peramalya's family is demanding answers regarding his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using the country as a dumping ground. The arrangement has raised questions regarding how much the UK government should disclose about such deals and how it protects both the individuals sent overseas and the communities that receive them. In contrast to the UK's current undisclosed arrangement, five EU countries have reached a deal to send people whose asylum claims have been refused to Rwanda.

cards.headline: Eight finalists announced for inaugural Children's Booker Prize

pages.text: The Booker Prize Foundation has revealed the eight shortlisted finalists for its first-ever Children's Booker Prize. Dubbed the “Great Eight,” the shortlist includes five novels, two graphic novels, and an illustrated collection of short stories intended for readers aged eight to 12. The finalists were selected from 89 submissions published in the United Kingdom or Ireland, featuring authors and illustrators from five countries across three continents. A panel of four young judges will decide the winner of the £50,000 (approximately $65,500) award in February. Children's author and screenwriter Frank Cottrell-Boyce is chairing the judging panel. Cottrell-Boyce stated that the panel's guiding rule was to ensure every book on the shortlist was “truly FOR CHILDREN.”

The Booker Prize Foundation launched this new award following concerns regarding declining youth reading habits. According to Britain’s Annual Literacy Survey from 2025, the proportion of children and teenagers who enjoy reading fell to one in three, the lowest level recorded in the 20 years since the survey began tracking the metric. The Children's Booker Prize serves as a counterpart to the adult Booker Prize, a prestigious fiction honor established in 1969. The announcement follows the 2026 adult Booker Prize win by M. John Harrison for *The End of Everything*.

cards.headline: Spaceflight alters Alzheimer’s-related biological processes differently based on genetic background

pages.text: Researchers at the University of California San Diego have found that spaceflight alters biological processes associated with Alzheimer’s disease in different ways depending on an individual's genetic background. A study published Nov. 25, 2026, in Science Advances suggests that the environment of space could reveal changes in brain cells that are difficult to detect on Earth. This research may help scientists understand how different genetic forms of the disease respond to stress, potentially leading to more targeted treatments for Alzheimer's, which affects more than 55 million people worldwide and is projected to reach 139 million by 2050.

To study the disease, researchers grew brain organoids, which are small, three-dimensional neural tissue models derived from stem cells that reproduce some features of the human brain. Because the earliest stages of Alzheimer's are difficult to study in living human brains, these models allow for closer observation of the disease's mechanisms, such as synapse loss, the buildup of amyloid-beta protein plaques, and changes to the tau protein that supports nerve cells. In the study, some organoids carried mutations in APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2—three genes linked to rare inherited forms of Alzheimer’s—while others served as controls without those mutations.

Alysson R. Muotri, PhD, a professor in the Departments of Pediatrics and Cellular & Molecular Medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the Sanford Integrated Space Stem Cell Orbital Research Center at the UC San Diego Sanford Stem Cell Institute, noted that Alzheimer’s is often discussed as if it follows one predictable path. Muotri stated that the findings suggest different genetic forms may respond very differently to the same stress.

cards.headline: Vaporized rock reveals titanium oxide around massive young star

pages.text: Scientists have observed titanium oxide in gas form around a massive, young star for the first time. This discovery allows researchers to determine the composition of solid materials outside of our solar system without collecting physical samples to bring back to Earth. By observing vaporized rock, astronomers can identify the chemical makeup of solid objects in space through their gaseous remains.  The research team used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to observe this phenomenon in the disk of Orion Source I, a massive, young star located in a dusty cloud behind the Orion Nebula. The findings are published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The observation functions similarly to a laboratory experiment where material is blasted and evaporated to be measured by a spectrograph. Adam Ginsburg, a University of Florida associate professor of astronomy, identified the system examined by the team and developed some of the techniques used to analyze it. Ginsburg noted that while mineralogists have long examined rocks on Earth, scientists have previously been unable to study solids in this manner within the interstellar medium. He stated that the discovery provides a way to understand what solid objects in space are made of because nature is effectively performing the evaporation and measurement process in space.
